extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental scientists, and investigators of nature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, carrying out, and interpreting experiments in natural philosophy: how to render imperceptible phenomena sensible, measure magnitudes (space/time/quantity/predominance), avoid experimental fallacies, and choose practical instances that make theory useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to the sensible sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring objects not naturally perceivable by human senses into the sphere of the senses by contrivances or procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical contrivances and procedures (e.g., distillation, evaporation into a bladder, thermometric effects) to convert imperceptible entities into perceptible forms so they can be measured and compared. Examples: converting spirituous liquid to vapor to compare volumes; using expansion/contraction of air to register heat/cold. Emphasize careful measurement of before-and-after weights/volumes. Beware that reduction is not proof of original internal state without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments to avoid induced artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that experimental agents (heat, separating media, violent procedures) can superinduce qualities not originally present, producing fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly violent or energetic methods that destroy delicate conformations or introduce new qualities (e.g., qualities created by fire in distillation). When using separations, check whether observed products were created by the method rather than preexisting in the specimen. Use milder, more natural imitations when possible and seek corroborating instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use instruments and contrivances to extend human senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ physical devices and measures (thermometers, vessels, bladders, glass) to render subtle phenomena observable and measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct small-scale, controlled contrivances to concentrate effects and reduce required heat or material (example: small vial for vapor expansion experiment). Prefer setups that allow precise weighing and observation before and after. Choose scale and materials to minimize artefacts and make subsequent operations (e.g., evaporation) easier and less destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ other animals' senses when human senses are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: When human senses cannot perceive a phenomenon (e.g., faint light, certain scents), consider organisms whose senses exceed those of humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use animals with superior capabilities (dogs for scent, cats/owls for night vision) as supplementary observers, while recognizing differences in sensory relation to phenomena. Treat such evidence as complementary and subject to further confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make imperceptible motions sensible by accumulation or measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Slow or fast motions imperceptible to direct observation must be rendered perceptible by accumulation, slowing, or precise measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very slow motions, observe cumulative effects (e.g., growth by periodically pulling seeds). For very rapid motions (e.g., musket-ball), develop measurement techniques to capture velocity or infer effects from indirect evidence. Acknowledge that some velocities have not been well measured and require deliberate measurement methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce overpowering stimuli by distance, medium, or reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: When an object's effect on senses is too strong, lessen or alter its impact by moving it away, interposing a medium, or using its reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent sensory overload (e.g., glare from the sun), observe reflections or work through attenuating media. Similarly, interpose materials to deaden strong forces to measure them safely and meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use supplementary or substitutive instances by approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct instances cannot be obtained, use approximate substitutes that differentially attenuate or reveal effects (comparative media or thicknesses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare how a phenomenon propagates through different media to infer properties (e.g., magnetism through gold vs air). Such approximation-by-degree can indicate relative susceptibilities or limits. Note examples and perform controlled comparisons; do not overinterpret approximate results as exact equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substitution by analogy with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct perception is impossible, use analogous, perceptible systems to form hypotheses about the imperceptible, but treat analogies as less certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map perceptible mixtures (oil and water) onto imperceptible mixtures (flame and air) to generate hypotheses. Investigate whether the analogy holds (e.g., whether spirituous bodies mix like liquids). Validate analogical inferences by focused experiments before acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and observe processes over time (itinerant/road instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe nature during its operation, not only initial materials and finished products; watch gradual continuities and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up regular, frequent observations (e.g., inspect seeds daily, watch hatching) to capture stages of development. Use small, repeated sampling to infer continuous processes. Prefer process observations to static end-state inspection to understand mechanism and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical instances and instances of measure (account for space/time/quantity/predominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and measure the four circumstances that determine practical efficacy of powers: space (extent), time (moments), quantity at a given period (dose), and predominance (relative strength).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, ensure experiments quantify these four variables to avoid deceptive or impractical theories. Use measurement to determine limits, scales, rates, and comparative strengths so that theoretical results are applicable in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer propitious (benevolent) instances to reduce labor and focus practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Select instances that make practice less laborious: those that limit instruments or matter needed, or direct work to what matters most to mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose experiments that economize resources (smaller scales, fewer instruments) and prioritize phenomena of consequence. Seek instances that both demonstrate the principle and are practical to implement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the rod/rule (measure limits and distances of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the definite spatial limits within which powers act—whether by contact or at a distance—and note how they vary by medium, mass, and vigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure distances at which effects operate (e.g., magnetic attraction, light, perfume, heat). Distinguish contact-only effects from distant actions and document boundaries. Use tools (telescopes, barriers) to extend or constrain effective ranges and to reveal limits relevant to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure spherical motion: compression and expansion limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how bodies expand or compress (spherical motion), determining degrees before resistance or rupture occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform controlled compression/expansion experiments (examples: immersed bell, leaden globe with water pressed in, glass egg suction) to quantify compressibility and elasticity. Note when escape occurs by bursting or leakage and measure thresholds rather than assume. Distinguish behavior of rarefied vs tangible bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the course (measure by time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure natural actions by definite moments of time; consider absolute and relative time measures for motion and phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record durations, rates, and relative timings (e.g., light vs sound, projectile flight) to understand dynamics. Use timing to explain effects (e.g., why quick motions can overcome larger but slower resistances). Consider both absolute times and relative temporal relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider relative measures of motion and velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare velocities of interacting phenomena to explain dominance or outcomes (e.g., expansion of gunpowder vs gravity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze which motion occurs first or faster, since a rapid action can outrun a slower opposing force and determine the resultant effect. Apply this to practical demonstrations (mines, projectiles) and biological control (small active spirits controlling large masses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe order of effects: first and last in processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which constituents or properties are extracted or manifested first and which appear later during a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track sequential extraction in infusions and distillations (e.g., in violet infusion, sweet odor first then earthy part; in distillation, watery phlegm first, aroma last). Use staged or repeated short extractions to maximize desired components and plan timing for optimal results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of quantity (doses): measure effect as function of quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how the quantity of a body affects its power and the required dose for an effect; do not assume linear proportionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentally determine exact proportions and doses (e.g., magnetism scale, concentration effects in fermentations). Beware naive proportional extrapolations (double mass does not imply double speed) and measure empirically for each power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of wrestling (predominance): determine comparative strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: When powers combine, identify which predominates and which submits; analyze compounded and opposed motions to determine effective power relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify active motions (resistance of matter, motion of connection to prevent vacuum, etc.) and perform comparative experiments to reveal which power wins under given conditions. Use controlled competitions of forces to establish hierarchies of predominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lancing (twitching) instances to awaken observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use striking, small-scale phenomena that reveal exquisite subtleties of nature to rouse attention and prompt further inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and present remarkable examples (ink drawing many letters, strong perfume spreading, minute worms with complex conformation) to stimulate careful observation. Pair such instances with measurements and limits to form deeper inductive leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note that similar natures may extinguish each other; measure interaction limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that actions of similar nature can subdue or extinguish one another (e.g., sunlight extinguishes candlelight), and document these interaction limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify contexts where like phenomena interfere and where different phenomena coexist without interference (e.g., many types of impressions pass through air simultaneously). Study boundaries and conditions under which one action overcomes another to inform practical application.
